paragraphs: In certain remote corners of the Old World you may still stumble on a small district that seems to have been forgotten in the general tumult and to have stood still while everything around it was in motion. The inhabitants are for the most part extremely ignorant and poor. They take no part in the affairs of the country, and the government often oppresses them. Yet their faces are generally calm and their spirits light. In America I saw the freest and best-educated men living in the happiest circumstances the world offers, and it seemed to me that a cloud habitually hung over their brows. I thought them serious and almost sad even in their pleasures. The chief reason for this contrast is that the former do not think about the ills they endure, while the latter are forever brooding over the advantages they lack. It is strange to see the feverish ardor with which the Americans pursue their own welfare, and to watch the vague dread that constantly torments them, the fear that they have not chosen the shortest path to it. A native of the United States clings to this world’s goods as if he were certain never to die. He is so hasty to seize everything within his reach that one would think he constantly feared he would not live long enough to enjoy it. He clutches at everything and holds nothing fast, but soon loosens his grasp to chase fresh gratifications.

In the United States a man builds a house to spend his later years in, and sells it before the roof is on. He plants a garden and rents it out just as the trees are beginning to bear fruit. He brings a field into cultivation and leaves others to gather the crops. He takes up a profession and gives it up. He settles in a place and soon leaves it, to carry his changeable longings elsewhere. If his private affairs leave him any free time, he plunges at once into the whirlpool of politics. And if, at the end of a year of unceasing labor, he finds he has a few days’ vacation, his eager curiosity sweeps him across the vast expanse of the United States, and he will travel fifteen hundred miles in a few days to shake off his happiness. Death finally overtakes him, but before he has tired of his fruitless chase after that complete happiness which is forever on the wing.

At first sight there is something surprising in the strange unrest of so many happy men, restless in the midst of abundance. Yet the sight itself is as old as the world. What is new is to see a whole people provide an example of it. Their taste for physical gratifications must be regarded as the original source of the secret uneasiness that the actions of the Americans betray, and of the inconstancy of which they give fresh examples every day. A man who has set his heart exclusively on the pursuit of worldly welfare is always in a hurry, for he has only a limited time to reach it, to grasp it and to enjoy it. The memory of how short life is spurs him on constantly. Besides the good things he has, he imagines at every moment a thousand others that death will prevent him from trying if he does not try them soon. This thought fills him with anxiety, fear and regret, and keeps his mind in ceaseless agitation, which leads him to change his plans and his home again and again. Suppose that, in addition to the taste for physical well-being, there is a social condition in which laws and customs make no position permanent. That is a powerful further stimulus to this restless temper. Men will then be seen constantly changing their course, for fear of missing the shortest way to happiness. It is easy to see that men passionately bent on physical gratifications desire eagerly, but are also easily discouraged. Their final aim is to enjoy, so the means of reaching it must be quick and easy, or the trouble of getting the gratification would be greater than the gratification itself. Their usual frame of mind is therefore both ardent and slack, violent and enervated. Death is often less dreaded than persevering in continuous effort toward a single end.

Equality of conditions leads by a still more direct road to several of the effects I have described here. When all privileges of birth and fortune are abolished, when all professions are open to everyone, and a man’s own energy can bring him to the top of any of them, an easy and unlimited career seems to lie open to his ambition. He will readily persuade himself that he is born for no ordinary destiny. But this is a mistaken idea, which daily experience corrects. The same equality that allows every citizen to form these lofty hopes makes all citizens less able to realize them. It limits their powers on every side, while giving their desires freer scope. Not only are they themselves powerless, but at every step they meet immense obstacles that they did not see at first. They have swept away the privileges of some of their fellow creatures that stood in their way, but they have opened the door to universal competition. The barrier has changed its shape rather than its place. When men are nearly alike and all follow the same track, it is very difficult for any one of them to walk fast and force a way through the dense crowd that surrounds and presses on him. This constant struggle between the longings that spring from equality of conditions and the means it supplies to satisfy them harasses and wearies the mind.

It is possible to imagine men who have reached a degree of freedom that would content them completely. They would then enjoy their independence without anxiety and without impatience. But men will never establish an equality with which they can be content. However hard a people may try, it will never succeed in reducing all the conditions of society to a perfect level. Even if they unhappily reached that absolute and complete leveling down, the inequality of minds would still remain. That inequality comes directly from the hand of God and will forever escape the laws of man. However democratic the social state and political constitution of a people may be, then, it is certain that every member of the community will always find several points around him that rise above his own position, and we can foresee that he will keep his eyes doggedly fixed in that direction. When inequality of conditions is the common law of society, the most striking inequalities do not catch the eye. When everything is nearly on the same level, the slightest inequality is noticeable enough to hurt. Hence the desire for equality always becomes more insatiable as equality becomes more complete.

Among democratic nations men easily attain a certain equality of conditions, but they can never attain the equality they desire. It is always drawing back from them, yet without hiding from their sight, and as it draws back it draws them on. At every moment they think they are about to seize it, and at every moment it slips from their hold. They are near enough to see its charms but too far away to enjoy them, and they die before they have fully tasted its delights. To these causes we must attribute the strange melancholy that often haunts the inhabitants of democratic countries in the midst of their abundance, and the disgust with life that sometimes seizes them in calm and easy circumstances. In France people complain that the number of suicides is rising. In America suicide is rare, but insanity is said to be more common than anywhere else. These are all different symptoms of the same disease. The Americans, however uneasy they may be, do not end their lives, because their religion forbids it. Among them materialism may be said hardly to exist, despite the general passion for physical gratification. The will resists, but reason often gives way. In democratic ages pleasures are more intense than in aristocratic ages, and above all many more people share in them. But on the other hand, it must be admitted that man’s hopes and desires are more often crushed, the soul is more stricken and disturbed, and care itself is sharper.
